chunks: "Boards get tested at several points, and each gate catches a different class of defect.
At the fab, every bare board gets an electrical netlist test for opens and shorts, because a bad board is cheapest to catch before parts go on.
During assembly, inspection happens in line: solder paste inspection after printing, automated optical inspection after reflow, and X-ray for hidden joints like BGAs.
In-circuit test or flying probe touches test points and pads with probes to check for shorts, opens, wrong or missing components and component values, without even needing the board to boot.
Then functional test powers the board up and checks that it actually does its job: rails, clocks, communications, sensors, firmware.
Some products also get burn-in or thermal cycling to weed out early failures, and a final end-of-line check before packing.
The rule is to find defects as early and cheaply as possible, while using functional test as the final proof, because it's slower and diagnoses poorly.
And separate from all that, during development an engineer tests a prototype on the bench against the spec, which is validation rather than production test."
